newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Second Ariane-5 to launch "dummy" satellites.
newsitem.headline: Second Ariane-5 to launch "dummy" satellites.

text.p: Europe's second Ariane-5 rocket, due to be launched in mid-April 1997 at the earliest, will put two "dummy" satellites into orbit to try to demonstrate its reliability, space officials said on Thursday.

The first Ariane-5 rocket exploded less than 40 seconds after lift-off in June, destroying four uninsured scientific satellites worth $500 million and delivering a devastating setback to development of Western Europe's new-generation rocket.
Specialists in Kourou said the "dummy" satellites would cost less than $3 million.

"The objective of Ariane flight 502 is to demonstrate the rocket's capacity to launch double satellite payloads into Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)," said Jean-Marie Luton, director of the European Space Agency (ESA).
"We will launch two instrument platforms that represent satellite masses," Luton told a news conference in Paris broadcast to the ESA launch centre in French Guiana.

Luton said the explosion on the maiden Ariane-5 flight represented a financial loss of $350 million and set back the Ariane-5 programme by at least a year. Arianespace had planned to start using Ariane-5 for its customers in 1997.

"We are considering restructuring the programme's financing by a redistribution of Ariane-5's budget, more funding from member states and a contribution from the programme's industrial partners," Luton said.
The second and final Ariane-5 test flight was initially scheduled for this month but was pushed back to April 1997 and a third test flight has been ordered.
An inquiry board investigating the explosion concluded in July that the failure was caused by software design errors in a guidance system.

The Paris-based Arianespace company that launches the Ariane rocket series said it would order more flight proven Ariane-4 rockets. The company had initially planned to phase out the Ariane-4 and use only Ariane-5s by the year 2000.
"This transition period has now become delicate. We have taken the decision to order more Ariane-4 rockets," Arianespace president Charles Bigot said.
"I cannot now give you an exact number but I would estimate it to be about five or six to meet the demands of our clients scheduled for launch in 1999," he added.
Arianespace has on order 22 more Ariane-4 rockets and 14 Ariane-5 rockets to service a customer backload of 42 heavy satellites to launch worth an estimated $4.1 billion.
